chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from al-Husayn ibn Malik said:

I wrote to him: A man died and left all that he owned during his life to you, and he had no children. Then, after that, he had a child. The total amount of his wealth was three thousand dirhams, and I have sent to you one thousand dirhams. If you see fit, may God be my ransom, inform me of your opinion regarding this so that I may act upon it. He wrote: Release it to them. And these narrations are consistent with the preceding narrations and with what we added to them in our Great Book, so acting upon them is more appropriate. And if the preceding narrations were free from contradiction, they would encompass several interpretations: one being that the owner of the wealth commanded that the wealth be transferred to them not as a bequest, but as a gift during his lifetime. If that is the case, it is permissible according to what we presented in the earlier narrations. And only what was a bequest is returned to the one-third. The second is that the heirs of these people were differing in creed from him, so it was permissible to deprive them of that and transfer the wealth to the Imam. The third is that this was permissible because he made his bequest before they became his heirs, then a heir came to him who did not invalidate his bequest, and his bequest remained valid in its entirety, and it was not obligatory to invalidate it. This indicates that.

key_terms.الثُّلُث: The one-third portion of the estate allocated for bequests
key_terms.الْإِمَام: The Imam (in this context, the financial authority receiving the wealth)
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّة: Bequest (gift upon death, limited to one-third of estate)

ai.seo_question: How is a lifetime gift to the Imam distinguished from a bequest in Shia inheritance law?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the legal distinction between a lifetime gift (*hibah* or *silah*) and a posthumous bequest (*wasiyyah*), ruling that wealth designated to the Imam during life transfers fully rather than being limited to the one-third share reserved for bequests. The text provides three scholarly interpretations for this ruling, including the possibility that the heirs were excluded due to doctrinal differences (*ikhtilaf fi al-i'tiqad*) or that the bequest was made before heirs existed, thus remaining valid. This highlights the Imam's authority to determine the nature of the transfer and the conditions under which heirs may be disinherited.
